title: Hosted API demo - Chat & text generation basics (streaming, params, retries)
summary: Redwood demo of Hosted API focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming responses, key params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and retry/backoff behavior. Customer Lark Ventures is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a consumer-facing chat feature; main concerns are latency, cost, and data retention. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with benchmark prompts and provide security docs and pricing. Action items assigned.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-21
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Lark - Head of Product), Tom Delgado (Lark - ML Eng), Priya Singh (Lark - CTO)

Auto-summary: quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat streaming, parameter tuning and retry behavior. Customer asked about latency/cost tradeoffs and data retention. Agreed pilot and follow ups.

00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this account, and with me is Jordan, our solutions engineer. How are you all doing?
00:07 Aisha (Lark): Good thanks, excited to see this. We got a short agenda in the invite — just want to make sure we cover streaming and the params, and also how retries work cause we worry about duplicated outputs.
00:17 Jordan (Redwood SE): Totally, we'll demo the hosted API endpoints for chat and text generation, show streaming, and then dive into headers/params you can tune. We'll also show the Console briefly and touch on Redwood Optimize suggestions.
00:29 Priya (Lark): Great. Quick context — we're building an in-app chat assistant, mostly short responses but occasionally longer summaries. Latency is pretty important, and we have a strict cost vector. Also legal wants to know about data retention and encryption.
00:42 Jordan: Understood. For hosted, data is encrypted at rest and in transit; we have KMS integrations for dedicated/private but for hosted we can share the security pack with retention defaults and options. We'll get that to you after the call.
00:55 Tom (Lark): On latency: what kind of token-per-second and p95 latencies should we expect for chat? We're mostly low concurrencies but spikes at peak.
01:05 Jordan: Typical p95 for a standard gpt-ish open model on our hosted tier is in the 150-400ms per-token range for 1k-context, but it varies by model and payload. For short chat turns (80-150 tokens) end-to-end latency will often be sub-second to a couple seconds, streaming can help perceived latency because you get early tokens immediately.
01:27 Maya: I'll quickly share my screen and run through a demo.
01:32 [screen share begins]
01:39 Jordan: Alright, sending a chat completion request — here's the REST call: POST /v1/chat/completions with messages array, model param, and a stream=true flag for SSE. If stream is true you'll get an event stream where chunks come as they're generated.
01:52 Jordan: (typing) First try streaming=false so you see the full response.
02:05 Jordan: Sample payload includes temperature (0.0-1.0), top_p, max_tokens, and a stop sequence. For deterministic behaviors choose low temperature and top_p; for creative responses bump them up.
02:18 Aisha: Can you show a concrete example for something like a user question -> short reply?
02:22 Jordan: Sure. Prompt: "What's the best way to reset a password?" max_tokens 80 temperature 0.2. (runs) And here's the output.
02:35 [output appears]
02:40 Tom: Looks good. If we set stream=true how do retries behave? If a connection drops mid-stream do we get partial duplication or is there an idempotency key?
02:51 Jordan: Good question. For hosted API we recommend using an idempotency key header for requests that cause side-effects, but for generation requests typically we do best-effort. If the connection drops while streaming, you can re-issue the same request with the same idempotency key — Redwood will try to return an equivalent result but due to non-determinism you might get slightly different tokens. For strict dedupe we suggest using the non-streaming path or caching the last n tokens on client side. There's also an at-least-once/at-most-once nuance depending on how you implement retries.
03:21 Priya: So retries can cause duplicated completions in our UI if we're not careful?
03:25 Jordan: Yes, if you blindly re-display the full response you'll see duplicates. Best practice is to buffer partial chunks and reconcile on reconnects, or do a non-stream retry and compare. We have SDK helpers that manage reconnection and dedup heuristics — we'll share those.
03:40 Aisha: What's the retry/backoff policy you recommend? Exponential backoff with jitter?
03:44 Jordan: Exactly, exponential backoff with randomized jitter. For most customers we suggest initial retry after 500ms, then 1s, 2s, 4s and stop after a set number or a total time budget. If you expect transient network issues at the client side, tune the max retries accordingly.
03:59 Maya: Switching to Console for a second — here is the per-route dashboard and latency histogram. You can set traffic shaping and route low-latency traffic to higher-tier models or dedicated capacity.
04:14 Jordan: Also calling out Redwood Optimize — it will analyze token distribution and suggest quantization or batching settings to save cost. For chat workloads Optimize suggests prefix caching where applicable.
04:28 Tom: How does prefix caching work for session-based chat? We have multi-turn threads and don't want to re-send entire context every time.
04:35 Jordan: We support prefix/KV cache on the server side for pinned sessions; you can also use partial context via cache keys so that repeated system instructions or user profiles aren't re-sent. For hosted, caching is automatic for frequently repeated prefixes and we expose hit/miss metrics in the Console. That can significantly lower tokens consumed.
04:56 Aisha: About params — do you recommend tuning temperature or top_p first?
05:01 Jordan: Start with temperature for tone control. If you need to restrict sampling further, top_p can complement temperature. Also max_tokens and logits_bias can shape output length and content. We typically run small A/Bs with a held-out prompt set to measure quality vs hallucination. Redwood has eval hooks to automate that.
05:21 [Jordan runs a streaming example]
05:28 Jordan: I'm turning stream=true now. You should see token chunks coming over SSE.
05:35 [SSE stream begins: tokens arrive in chunks]
05:42 Aisha: Nice, I can see it populating live — perceived latency feels much lower.
05:47 Priya: If we need guaranteed reproducibility for a specific user-facing response, is the only way to do that to set temperature=0 and seed?
05:57 Jordan: Temperature=0 helps determinism but not always fully deterministic across model versions/quantizations. For strict reproducibility across runs you should pin model version and use the same model weights + deterministic sampling. For hosted that's possible by pinning to a specific model version in your request.
06:13 Tom: Cost question — how do you price streaming vs non-streaming? Is it token-based all the same?
06:19 Maya: Pricing is token-based for both. Streaming just changes delivery; you still pay for tokens generated. But because streaming lets you stop earlier (user cuts off), you can sometimes reduce tokens charged in practice. Our pricing sheet has per-input and per-output token rates and discounts for committed usage.
06:35 Aisha: Can you talk about rate limits and concurrency — we might have spikes when a campaign goes live.
06:41 Jordan: Hosted tier has per-key rate limits and burst windows, and we expose quota settings on the Console. For predictable spikes we recommend reserved/dedicated capacity which gives you guaranteed concurrency. For initial pilots, hosted usually suffices, and you can use smart routing and fallback model variants if capacity is constrained.
06:58 Priya: About data retention — legal wants clarity. Where are logs kept, and do you retain prompt/response for more than X days?
07:06 Maya: By default hosted retains logs for 30 days for debugging, but you can opt into shorter retention or opt-out for specific data classes. For enterprises we have Private deployments and Dedicated where retention policies and KMS-managed keys are available. We'll send the SOC2/ISO and a retention options doc.
07:25 Tom: For the pilot, will we be able to stream metrics into our observability — like token counts per request?
07:31 Jordan: Yes, Console exposes per-request token counts and there's a tracing hook so you can forward logs or integrate via our API. We also provide a lightweight agent for shipping traces to Datadog or your system.
07:44 Aisha: One more technical: how do you recommend handling stop sequences for multi-turn dialogues? Sometimes the assistant keeps talking beyond the slot.
07:52 Jordan: Use explicit stop sequences when you can, or set a conservative max_tokens. Another trick is to append a sentinel token at the end of system prompts and stop on that. We can show examples in the guide.
08:05 [screen: Jordan opens an example repo in Console & shows code snippets for SDK calls]
08:12 Jordan: Here's the Node SDK example; it wraps streaming read and does dedup checks. It also exposes a reconnect handler that uses the idempotency header and will try to reconcile partial streams.
08:25 Aisha: This is helpful. If we do the pilot, what do you need from us to get realistic benchmarks?
08:30 Jordan: We need a representative prompt set (20-50 prompts across short/long), traffic profile (QPS and concurrency), expected SLA (p95 latency goal) and any regulatory constraints. We'll run the tests and return a benchmark report.
08:45 Maya: Quick recap and next steps — we'll send pricing & security docs, Jordan will send the benchmark harness and sample prompts, and Lark will share their prompt set and traffic estimates. Plan pilot kickoff next week.
08:57 Priya: Sounds good — one ask from Legal: can Redwood provide an encryption-at-rest summary and details on who can access logs?
09:05 Maya: Absolutely, we'll include that in the security pack.
09:10 Aisha: Cool, thanks everyone — excited to run this.
09:14 [call ends]

Notes on transcription quality: some technical terms were transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV cache" sometimes appears as "K V cache" and "idempotency" once typed as "idem potency"), proper nouns like product features occasionally mis-capitalized. Natural speech artifacts (uh, mm, overlaps) were kept to preserve realism.
